newsitem.title: CANADA: Laidlaw to benefit from Allied Waste sale.
newsitem.headline: Laidlaw to benefit from Allied Waste sale.

text.p: Allied Waste Industries Inc. agreed Wednesday to buy Laidlaw Inc.'s solid waste management unit for $1.65 billion in an arrangement which analysts said benefits Laidlaw.
"I think it's an extremely attractive deal," said Griffiths McBurney analyst Greg Misztela.

The acquisition will make Scottsdale, Ariz.-based Allied the nation's fourth-largest solid waste company, with annual 1996 revenues of $1 billion. Allied Waste reported 1995 revenues of $169.9 million.
It will do business in 23 states and seven Canadian provinces, with 49 landfills, 115 collection locations and 29 transfer stations.

Under terms of the deal, Toronto-based Laidlaw, which also owns school bus and ambulance services, will receive $1.2 billion in cash, a 7 percent, 12-year subordinated debenture with a face amount of $150 million, and a 12-year subordinated note with a face amount of $168 million, Allied said.

Laidlaw, which will continue to own a hazardous waste business, will also receive 14.6 million shares of Allied Waste common stock and 20.4 million warrants for the stock. It will end up holding 20 percent of Allied Waste common stock.
The deal was approved by the boards of both companies.

Laidlaw, which has been carrying out acquisitions of its own this year, may not have finished shopping, according to Chief Executive James Bullock. "We have capacity for opportunities that will come along," he said in an interview.
One possible Laidlaw target is American Medical Response Inc., which would complement Laidlaw's ambulance service business, said Dunnery Best, an analyst with Richardson Greenshields of Canada.
American Medical Response Chief Executive Howard Siegel said his company was not in talks with Laidlaw but did not rule out future negotiations.
"I think there's some synergism," he said in a telephone interview.
Laidlaw earlier this year swallowed the transportation division of Scott's Hospitality Inc., consolidating its position as North America's largest school bus company.
But Misztela said Laidlaw would more likely concentrate on smaller companies.
"American Medical Response is a relatively large company right now and a little bit bigger than Laidlaw's operations. There's several smaller operations that they could go after," Misztela said.
"I think they're going to be using the cash prudently," Misztela said.
In its third quarter, Laidlaw reported revenues of C$818 million ($597 million) for the three months ended May 31.

Laidlaw was the most actively traded share on the Toronto Stock Exchange Wednesday. Its class B shares rose C$1.25 (91 cents) to close at C$15.55 ($11.34), with 8.4 million shares traded. The stock is trading at its highest since 1991, Best said.

Best added that "in recent years, (Laidlaw) has managed to maintain an excellent record of growth through acquisition as it refocused on two main areas: transport, with ambulances and school buses, and toxic waste handling." He added that Laidlaw's shares were still rated a buy, with a target price of C$18 ($13.12) within a year.

The Standard & Poor's rating agency said Wednesday that it had revised Laidlaw's outlook to stable from negative. It also affirmed its ratings on the company's senior unsecured debt and corporate credit ratings at triple-B-plus.
Allied Waste stock rose 37.5 cents to $9.50 on Nasdaq.
